strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous experimental validation across 5 datasets, 2 architectures, and multiple settings (batch, online, long sequences, domain shift) with consistent improvements and thorough ablations
Significant practical speedups demonstrated (up to 90%+ reduction in post-extraction training time) with competitive or improved accuracy, addressing an important deployment concern
Well-motivated problem formulation (multicollinearity in representation-based CL) with clear visualization of progressive decorrelation across pipeline stages (Figure 3)
Theoretical grounding through Theorems 4.1-4.2 providing formal analysis of sparse projection and top-k sparsification with information preservation guarantees
Strong reproducibility support with detailed algorithms, training details, multiple random seeds, error bars, and promised code release
weaknesses: Limited novelty in core components—sparse random projection, top-k sparsification, ridge regression, and GCV are established techniques; novelty is primarily in combination and application, representing an engineering rather than conceptual contribution

Data normalization confounds comparisons—Table 7 shows normalization provides 93.89%-91.64%=2.25% accuracy gain on ViT-B/16 CIFAR-100, orthogonal to decorrelation contribution, making it difficult to isolate Fly-CL's specific impact

Feature extraction dominates execution time—τpost (5.38s) is only 28% of τtrain (19.07s) on ViT-B/16 CIFAR-100; practical speedup is limited without parallelizing feature extraction, and quantization is treated as secondary

Biological motivation appears post-hoc—authors acknowledge KC→MBON decorrelation theory is 'inconclusive' (p.2), and ridge regression modeling may not be biologically faithful; motivation doesn't fundamentally shape algorithm design

Incomplete analysis of when/why the method works—no investigation of which datasets benefit most from decorrelation, static correlation visualization in Figure 3, weak theoretical connection between prototype correlation and classification accuracy

Hyperparameter selection lacks principled guidance—default values (m=10,000, p=300, k=3,000) appear arbitrary, and penalty coefficient range selection requires prior knowledge of multicollinearity rather than principled selection criteria

Baseline comparisons have limitations—prompt-based methods not evaluated on CNNs by design, F-OAL degradation on ResNet-50 may be implementation-specific, and detailed comparison with closest baseline (RanPAC) is superficial

strengths: Addresses practical efficiency problem in continual learning with substantial computational speedups (e.g., 91% reduction in post-extraction training time on CIFAR-100)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (5), architectures (2), and settings (CIL, online CL, domain shifts) with detailed ablations
Well-documented implementation with clear hyperparameters, experimental setup, and reproducibility considerations
Good component-level efficiency analysis (Table 4) showing how each optimization contributes to speedup
Adaptive regularization via GCV is a practical improvement over grid search for large-dimensional problems
weaknesses: Weak theoretical justification for KC→MBON mapping to ridge regression—connection is post-hoc; paper acknowledges 'clear theory has yet to be established' then proposes ridge regression without biological or principled justification
Limited technical novelty—combines existing techniques (sparse random projection from RanPAC, ridge regression, top-k sparsification, GCV) with solid engineering but minimal conceptual contribution

Data normalization is a major confounding factor (Table 7): 2.25% gain from normalization alone on CIFAR-100; unclear how much of reported improvement is due to architecture-specific normalization vs. proposed method

Incomplete decorrelation analysis—Figure 3 shows correlations heatmaps without quantitative metrics; marginal improvement from stage (b) to (c); no validation that decorrelation actually explains performance gains
Feature extraction dominates runtime (72-86% of wall-clock time in Tables 1-2), significantly reducing practical speedup claims; paper mentions quantization could help but doesn't demonstrate
Modest improvements over strongest baseline (RanPAC): worse on CIFAR-100 (93.89 vs 94.21), marginal on CUB (~1.17%), only significant on VTAB (2.38%); inconsistent performance gains
Claims of 'biologically plausible' and 'bio-inspired' are overstated—PN→KC mapping is reasonable but KC→MBON→ridge regression lacks proper biological justification
Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 are correct but standard—sparse matrix rank preservation and Lipschitz-based performance bounds are well-known techniques without novel insights
Hyperparameter choices (m=10,000, p=300, k=3,000) appear arbitrary; sensitivity analysis provided but lacks principled justification across different datasets
Code link incomplete (Abstract states 'Code is available at' with no URL); reproducibility reliant on author cooperation

strengths: Substantial practical efficiency improvements (60-90% speedup in post-extraction training time) consistently demonstrated across diverse datasets, backbones, and settings
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with thorough ablations, sensitivity analyses, and reproducibility (detailed pseudocode, training details, code availability promised)
Clear problem formulation of multicollinearity in representation-based CL with effective visualizations (Figure 3) showing progressive decorrelation through pipeline stages

Broad applicability across architectures (ViT, ResNet) and settings (batch, online, long sequences, severe domain shift) with well-integrated technical components (GCV adaptive regularization, Cholesky optimization)
Practical value for edge deployment avoiding model storage overhead compared to mixture-based approaches
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: each component (sparse random projection, top-k sparsification, ridge regression, streaming statistics) is established; main contribution is engineering their combination with incremental improvements

Loose biological motivation: paper acknowledges KC→MBON decorrelation evidence is 'inconclusive'; modeling via streaming ridge regression is significant abstraction; biological connection appears retrofitted rather than fundamentally inspiring algorithmic design

Unclear causal mechanism: multicollinearity shown to exist (Figure 3a) but not convincingly demonstrated as the main bottleneck addressed by method; improvements could stem from other factors (adaptive regularization, data normalization effects, sparse projection benefits)

Data normalization as confounding factor: Table 7 shows significant performance variation with architecture-specific normalization strategies; unclear if this normalization equally benefits all baseline methods, potentially explaining observed improvements

Incremental theoretical contributions: Theorem 4.1 applies standard results (Tao & Vu 2006); Theorem 4.2 makes strong assumptions (B.2, B.3) that may not hold after random projection, provides loose bounds, and lacks actionable guidance for hyperparameter selection

Inconsistent performance across settings: accuracy drops on CIFAR-100 (93.89% vs RanPAC's 94.21%); gains vary significantly by dataset (2-3% CIFAR-100 vs ~1% CUB); online CL shows smaller improvements than batch mode

Incomplete ablations: Figure 4 combines sparse projection and top-k without isolating individual contributions; missing ablation on adaptive GCV vs fixed regularization; no component-level contribution analysis beyond Table 4

Insufficient comparison with F-OAL: highly similar approach yet F-OAL competitive on CUB and VTAB without top-k operation; ResNet-50 degradation attributed to 'error accumulation' but lacks rigorous explanation for why sparse projection specifically helps

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (CIFAR-100, CUB-200-2011, VTAB, ImageNet-R/A), architectures (ViT-B/16, ResNet-50, Qwen2.5-VL-7B), and eight diverse baselines with proper metrics and ablations
Significant practical efficiency gains: 67-91% reduction in post-extraction training time while maintaining or improving accuracy across datasets
Solid theoretical analysis with rigorous complexity bounds (Theorems 4.1-4.2) and elegant connection between Hebbian learning and ridge classification (Section 6)
Strong reproducibility with detailed experimental protocols, hyperparameter justification, sensitivity analyses, and public dataset availability
Well-motivated framework design with clear visualization of decorrelation effects (Figures 2-3) and comprehensive ablation studies (Figures 4-5)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: sparse random projection, top-k sparsification, and ridge regression are all standard techniques; primary contribution is their combination, which is incremental for a top-tier venue

Theoretical contributions are incremental: Theorems 4.1-4.2 build on well-known random matrix theory (Tao & Vu, 2006) and standard statistical learning theory; Theorem 6 is a straightforward equivalence proof rather than a deep insight

Biological plausibility claims are overstated: the fixed random projection matrix W lacks learning/plasticity; top-k thresholding is a crude approximation of lateral inhibition; KC→MBON theory (Section 6) shows mathematical equivalence to ridge regression, not biological replication

Fairness concerns in experiments: (1) all baselines forced to use Fly-CL's normalization strategy, which provides 2-3% boost (Table 7) and may not reflect original paper results; (2) F-OAL's anomalously poor performance on ResNet-50 (66.63%) lacks detailed analysis; unclear if baselines were properly tuned with this constraint

Incomplete analysis of key mechanisms: Figure 3 shows decorrelation occurs but no rigorous evidence it is the primary driver of CL performance gains; no comparison with alternative decorrelation methods (PCA, ICA, ZCA whitening); design choices (Pearson correlation metric, GCV vs. alternatives for λ selection, m=10,000) lack full justification
Missing statistical rigor: results include ±std but no significance tests; some improvements marginal (0.32% on CIFAR-100); unclear if differences are statistically significant
Limited ablation scope: no empirical comparison of dense vs. sparse projection; alternative k-selection strategies unexplored; different correlation measures for multicollinearity not investigated
